title_full_ar: الجامع المسند الصحيح المختصر من أمور رسول الله ﷺ وسننه وأيامه
subject: hadith
summary: Sahih al-Bukhari is the most authoritative collection of hadith in the Sunni tradition, compiled by Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari (194–256 AH / 810–870 CE) after reportedly examining over 600,000 narrations and selecting approximately 7,563 (with repetitions) that met his rigorous conditions of authenticity. It is the second most revered text in Islam after the Qur'an.
overview:
Sahih al-Bukhari holds an unrivalled position in the hadith sciences. Its full title — al-Jami' al-Musnad al-Sahih al-Mukhtasar min Umur Rasul Allah wa Sunanihi wa Ayyamihi ('The Abridged Collection of Authentic Hadiths with Connected Chains Regarding the Affairs, Practices, and Days of the Messenger of Allah') — reflects Imam al-Bukhari's ambition: not merely to record narrations, but to produce a legal and theological reference structured around the fiqh of the Sunnah.

Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari was born in Bukhara (present-day Uzbekistan) in 194 AH / 810 CE. He began memorising hadith at the age of ten, travelled extensively across Iraq, the Hijaz, Syria, and Egypt, and reportedly studied under over one thousand scholars. His teacher Ishaq ibn Rahawayh is said to have suggested the need for a concise compilation of sound reports, inspiring the project.

Al-Bukhari spent sixteen years compiling the work and is reported to have performed two rak'ahs of prayer before recording each hadith. His primary criterion (shart) requires that each narrator in the chain (isnad) not only be of upright character (adl) and precise memory (dabt), but also that contemporaneous narrators in the chain must have demonstrably met — a condition more stringent than that of Imam Muslim, who required only the possibility of meeting. Al-Bukhari applied this standard for the higher grades of his collection.

The work is organised into 97 kutub (books) covering the major topics of Islamic jurisprudence and practice: purity, prayer, alms, fasting, pilgrimage, trade, inheritance, marriage, and many more, along with sections on Quranic exegesis (tafsir), the qualities of the Prophet ﷺ, the lives of the Companions, and eschatology. The organisation reveals al-Bukhari's legal acumen — his chapter headings (tarajim al-abwab) are often themselves brief fiqh positions implicit in the narrations he places beneath them.

The total count of hadith is approximately 7,563 including repetitions, with an estimated 2,602 unique narrations. Repetition is deliberate: al-Bukhari would place the same hadith under multiple chapter headings to derive distinct legal rulings from different aspects of the same text.

The definitive commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari is Fath al-Bari by Imam Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (d. 852 AH / 1449 CE), a work of approximately thirteen volumes that remains the standard scholarly reference. Ibn Hajar's commentary explains al-Bukhari's chapter headings, reconciles apparent contradictions, grades narrators, and provides exhaustive legal analysis. Other important commentaries include Umdah al-Qari by Imam Badr al-Din al-Ayni (d. 855 AH) and Irshad al-Sari by al-Qastallani (d. 923 AH).

The most widely used printed edition is the Dar al-Sha'b / Dar al-Hadith edition (Cairo), based on the Sultan Abd al-Hamid edition, and the Dar Tawq al-Najah edition edited by Muhammad Zuhayr ibn Nasir al-Nasir (Beirut, 2002), which is considered the most critically edited modern text. The standard English translation is by Dr. Muhammad Muhsin Khan (published by Darussalam), available in nine volumes. An earlier complete translation by M. Asad (Muhammad Leopold Weiss) exists for historical reference.

The status of Sahih al-Bukhari in the Islamic tradition extends beyond its technical hadith content. Generations of scholars completed the work in forty or sixty sittings as a blessed undertaking (khatm). Jurists across all four madhabs treated it as a primary evidentiary source. The great Hanbali scholar Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali (d. 795 AH) wrote Fath al-Bari ala Sahih al-Bukhari, a separate early commentary that predates Ibn Hajar's, and Imam al-Nawawi began a commentary that was never completed. The work is available in full at sunnah.com and in critical Arabic text through the Dar Tawq al-Najah digital editions.
